origin: Coined by Theodore Roosevelt, when 'bully' was slang for 'excellent.'
note: Has nothing to do with bullying.

def: describing a quick, rough calculation done informally rather than carefully or precisely
ex: A back-of-the-envelope estimate suggests the project will cost about two million dollars.
Priya did some back-of-the-envelope math and realized the trip was affordable.

cloze.s: Using a quick ___ calculation, the engineer guessed the old bridge could hold forty trucks.

def: a win that brings little real benefit or satisfaction
ex: Winning the lawsuit was a hollow victory after legal fees swallowed the entire settlement.
The championship felt like a hollow victory with their captain injured in the final minute.

cloze.s: Beating his brother at chess was ___ for Tomás, since his brother had barely paid attention.

note: Close to a 'Pyrrhic victory,' which stresses that the win cost too much.

def: the principle that buyers are responsible for checking quality before purchasing
ex: At flea markets, caveat emptor applies, so inspect everything before you pay.
Buying a used car from a stranger online is a classic case of caveat emptor.

cloze.s: The seller offers no refunds or guarantees, so the rule here is ___.

origin: Latin for 'let the buyer beware.'
note: Consumer-protection laws now limit this principle in many places.

def: as an automatic, direct result of that very act or circumstance
ex: Under the club's rules, missing three meetings ipso facto ends your membership.
Being popular does not ipso facto make a policy wise.

cloze.s: Under the treaty, signing it ___ makes a country subject to the court's rulings.

origin: Latin for 'by the fact itself.'

def: something already done or decided, leaving those affected no choice but to accept it
ex: By the time residents heard about the new highway, it was a fait accompli.
The board presented the merger to employees as a fait accompli.

cloze.s: The manager signed the contract before consulting the team, presenting them with a ___.

origin: French for 'accomplished fact.'

def: the general spirit, mood and ideas typical of a particular period of history
ex: The novel captured the zeitgeist of the 1920s, with its jazz, wealth and restlessness.
The startup's success showed it understood the zeitgeist of remote work.

cloze.s: Few films capture the ___ of their era as well as that one captured the anxieties of the Cold War.

origin: German for 'time spirit.'
note: Often capitalized, as in German.

def: pleasure felt at someone else's misfortune or failure
ex: Fans of rival teams felt some schadenfreude when the champions lost in the first round.
There was quiet schadenfreude in the office when the boastful manager's project failed.

cloze.s: When the arrogant player tripped over his own feet while celebrating, the crowd couldn't hide its ___.

origin: German, from Schaden 'harm' and Freude 'joy.'

def: someone who is unwelcome or not accepted, especially a diplomat expelled by a host country
ex: After leaking the club's secrets, Liam became persona non grata at its meetings.
The government declared two diplomats persona non grata and ordered them to leave.

cloze.s: After selling the team's playbook to a rival, the former coach was ___ at the stadium.

origin: Latin for 'unwelcome person'; it is a formal term in diplomacy.

def: an outstanding performance or achievement that shows great skill
ex: The actor's performance as the aging king was a tour de force.
Her final thesis was a tour de force of careful research and clear writing.

cloze.s: Critics called the pianist's farewell concert a ___, the finest of her long career.

origin: French for 'feat of strength' or 'feat of skill.'

def: a final blow or event that ends something already weakened or failing
ex: The pandemic was the coup de grâce for the struggling neighborhood theater.
A late goal delivered the coup de grâce to the visiting team's hopes.

cloze.s: Years of falling sales had weakened the store, and the new online rival dealt the ___.

origin: French for 'stroke of mercy,' originally a blow that ended a wounded person's suffering.
note: Pronounced 'grahs'; 'gras' means 'fat' in French.

def: a typical way of working or doing something, especially a criminal's characteristic methods
ex: Detectives noticed that the burglaries all shared the same modus operandi.
Arriving early and overpreparing is Wei's usual modus operandi before big meetings.

cloze.s: The scams all followed the same ___: a fake charity email asking for gift cards.

origin: Latin for 'way of operating'; often shortened to M.O.

def: harmed or defeated by the very scheme one devised to hurt someone else
ex: The executive who pushed for strict expense audits was hoist with her own petard when auditors flagged her travel claims.
Diego wrote the tricky contract clause to trap his partner, then was hoist with his own petard when it was enforced against him.

cloze.s: The company that lobbied for tougher copyright rules was ___ when those rules blocked its own product launch.

origin: From Shakespeare's Hamlet; a petard was a small bomb used to blast open gates, which could blow up the person setting it.
note: 'Hoisted by one's own petard' is also common.

def: to criticize indirectly by praising so weakly that the approval actually sounds negative
ex: Calling the chef's new menu 'perfectly adequate,' the critic damned it with faint praise.
Priya's reference letter damned him with faint praise, noting only that he was always punctual.

cloze.s: Asked about the new hire, the manager said only that he 'tries hard,' which ___.

origin: From Alexander Pope's 'Epistle to Dr. Arbuthnot' (1735): 'Damn with faint praise, assent with civil leer.'

def: a person, bid or proposal put forward to test reactions or to hide someone's real plans
ex: Analysts suspected the minor candidate was a stalking horse, testing support before the real contender entered the race.
In the bankruptcy auction, the first bidder served as a stalking horse, setting a minimum price for the assets.

cloze.s: The small proposal to trim library hours was ___ for a much larger plan to close branches.

origin: Hunters once hid behind a horse, real or artificial, to creep close to game without being seen.

def: an honor or job that seems desirable but is likely to bring trouble to whoever accepts it
ex: Taking over the struggling project turned out to be a poisoned chalice for Hannah.
Many coaches see managing a team right after a legend retires as a poisoned chalice.

cloze.s: Everyone congratulated Wei on her promotion, but leading the failing division proved ___.

origin: Echoes 'our poison'd chalice' in Shakespeare's Macbeth (Act 1, Scene 7).
note: More common in British English, often used of leadership roles.

def: a promise, commitment or remark that could cause trouble or embarrassment later
ex: Promising zero layoffs for five years was a hostage to fortune the CEO soon regretted.
Liam avoids giving exact launch dates in interviews, unwilling to offer a hostage to fortune.

cloze.s: By publicly guaranteeing the bridge would open by June, the mayor handed critics ___.

origin: From Francis Bacon's essay 'Of Marriage and Single Life': 'He that hath wife and children hath given hostages to fortune.'

def: to gain an advantage over a rival by acting earlier or more quickly than they do
ex: By launching its app in spring, the startup stole a march on its larger competitors.
Fatima stole a march on the other applicants by submitting her portfolio a week early.

cloze.s: Our rivals ___ us by booking the best venue before we had even chosen a date.

origin: Originally military: to move troops unnoticed, gaining ground before the enemy realized it.

def: to be in the position of control or advantage over others in a situation
ex: With three job offers in hand, Jamal held the whip hand in the salary talks.
As the only supplier of the part, the factory holds the whip hand in every negotiation.

cloze.s: Once the landlord knew no other apartments were available, he ___ and raised the rent sharply.

def: to keep resisting a change or defeat that will probably happen anyway
ex: Video rental stores fought a rearguard action against streaming before most of them closed.
The committee is fighting a rearguard action to keep the old grading system.

cloze.s: Long after typewriters vanished elsewhere, a few loyal offices ___ against computers.

origin: A rearguard is the part of an army that protects its back while it retreats.

def: advice that is ideal in theory but too demanding to follow in practice
ex: Telling busy parents to cook every meal from scratch is a counsel of perfection.
Eight hours of sleep a night is a counsel of perfection for most new doctors.

cloze.s: Saving half your income is sound advice, but for low-wage workers it is ___.

origin: Originally Christian theology: advice, such as voluntary poverty, aimed at spiritual perfection rather than required of all believers.

def: to act or speak mainly to win popular applause rather than to achieve something serious
ex: The lawyer's dramatic speech played to the gallery but did little to persuade the judge.
Critics said the coach was playing to the gallery by blaming referees after every loss.

cloze.s: Instead of offering realistic plans, the candidate ___ with crowd-pleasing promises.

def: a small sign that hints at what is likely to happen in the future
ex: The drop in holiday bookings was a straw in the wind for the whole tourism industry.
Analysts saw the founder's sudden sale of her shares as a straw in the wind.

cloze.s: The first few empty storefronts downtown were ___, signaling the slowdown to come.

term: nail one's colors to the mast
def: to declare one's position publicly and firmly, making it impossible to back down later
ex: Early in the debate, Sofia nailed her colors to the mast in favor of a four-day week.
The company nailed its colors to the mast by pledging to use only recycled packaging.

cloze.s: Rather than staying neutral, the editor ___ and openly backed the new stadium.
cloze.a: nailed her colors to the mast

origin: A warship whose flag, or colors, was nailed to the mast could not lower it to surrender.

def: to take risks by acting near the limits of what is legal or acceptable
ex: The accountant's aggressive tax strategies sailed close to the wind, and auditors soon noticed.
Comedians who sail close to the wind risk offending part of their audience.

cloze.s: Their advertising claims ___; one more exaggeration and regulators would have stepped in.

note: Also 'sail near the wind.'

def: a difficult, awkward situation that is hard to handle without causing offense or harm
ex: Telling a major client that their project is over budget is a sticky wicket.
Deciding which longtime employee to let go was a sticky wicket for Olga.

cloze.s: Explaining to both families why the wedding was suddenly postponed was ___.

origin: From cricket: a pitch drying after rain makes the ball bounce unpredictably, making batting difficult.
note: Chiefly British, though also heard in American English.

def: to behave carelessly or dishonestly, especially with facts, rules or other people's trust
ex: The documentary played fast and loose with history, inventing entire conversations.
Investors sued the firm for playing fast and loose with their retirement savings.

cloze.s: The reporter was fired for ___ with quotations, changing what sources had actually said.

note: Usually followed by 'with': play fast and loose with the truth.

def: a law, rule or agreement that formally still exists but is no longer enforced or obeyed
ex: The town's ban on Sunday shopping has been a dead letter for decades.
Without money for inspectors, the new safety code could quickly become a dead letter.

cloze.s: Nobody has obeyed the office's no-snacks rule in years; it is ___.

note: Also literally a piece of mail that cannot be delivered or returned.

def: an essential condition; something absolutely necessary, without which another thing cannot exist
ex: For a translator, fluency in both languages is the sine qua non of the job.
Trust is the sine qua non of any lasting business partnership.

cloze.s: Steady funding is ___ for the research program; without it, nothing else matters.

origin: Latin for 'without which not.'

def: unique; so unusual that it forms a category of its own
ex: The musician's blend of jazz and folk was sui generis, impossible to imitate.
Legally, the dispute was sui generis, with no clear precedent to follow.

cloze.s: Critics struggled to label the novel; it was truly ___, unlike anything written before it.

origin: Latin for 'of its own kind.'

def: a statement or conclusion that does not logically follow from what came before it
ex: 'It's raining, so we should buy a new car' is a classic non sequitur.
Malik's remark about his vacation was a non sequitur in a meeting about budgets.

cloze.s: Asked about rising prices, the spokesperson praised the company's new logo, an obvious ___.

origin: Latin for 'it does not follow.'
note: Used both for faulty logic and for any abrupt, unrelated remark in conversation.

def: a passionate, heartfelt appeal or protest
ex: The teacher's open letter was a cri de coeur for smaller class sizes.
Critics called the singer's new album a cri de coeur about loneliness in big cities.

cloze.s: The nurses' emotional speech to the hospital board was ___ for more staff.

origin: French for 'cry of the heart.'
note: Standard French says 'cri du cœur'; English usually writes 'cri de coeur.'

def: a person or thing that someone especially dislikes, dreads or finds troublesome
ex: Spelling tests were Diego's bête noire throughout elementary school.
Paperwork is the bête noire of many small-business owners, who would rather serve customers.

cloze.s: Long, pointless meetings are Hannah's ___; she avoids them whenever she possibly can.

origin: French for 'black beast.'

def: a powerful adviser who shapes decisions from behind the scenes without holding official authority
ex: Though she held no title, the founder's sister was the company's éminence grise.
Historians describe the quiet aide as the éminence grise behind the governor's reforms.

cloze.s: Officially just a consultant, he was the ___ who quietly shaped every major decision the CEO made.

origin: French for 'gray eminence,' first used of Father Joseph, the gray-robed friar who advised Cardinal Richelieu.

def: a comprehensive philosophy or outlook on the world and humanity's place in it
ex: The novelist's Weltanschauung, shaped by years of war, colors every chapter of her work.
A year studying abroad reshaped Aisha's entire Weltanschauung.

cloze.s: To understand the philosopher's ethics, you must first grasp her broader ___.

origin: German, from Welt 'world' and Anschauung 'view, perception.'
note: Capitalized because all German nouns are; 'worldview' is the everyday English equivalent.

def: the shared pride, loyalty and team spirit felt among members of a group
ex: The demanding training camp built a strong esprit de corps among the rookies.
Weekly team lunches helped restore esprit de corps after the painful layoffs.

cloze.s: The nurses' ___ was obvious: they covered each other's shifts and celebrated each other's wins.

origin: French for 'spirit of the body,' meaning the group as a whole.

def: to offer unwanted advice or comments, especially while watching others play a game
ex: Grandpa loves to kibitz at the chess tables in the park, critiquing every move.
Please don't kibitz while I'm working on the crossword; I want to solve it myself.

cloze.s: Onlookers crowded around the card table to ___, suggesting plays no one had asked for.

origin: Yiddish, from German kiebitzen 'to look on at cards,' from Kiebitz, the lapwing, a noisy bird.
note: Also means to chat or joke casually; a person who does it is a kibitzer.
